concept.name: Order rejection
concept.definition: The refusal of an order by the broker, exchange, or counterparty before or after acceptance, so that the order never becomes (or ceases to be) executable. Rejections carry a reason - invalid parameters, risk limits, insufficient margin, closed market, or duplicate identifiers.
concept.intuition: A rejection is the market saying 'no' at the door: nothing was executed and nothing rests - you must fix the problem and resubmit.
concept.mechanics: The venue returns a reject message with a reason code (in FIX, an Execution Report with ExecType/OrdStatus = Rejected plus an OrdRejReason field; Cboe rejects for duplicates, orders outside trading hours, or stale NBBO conditions). An order can even be rejected after an earlier acknowledgment - status can pass from New to Rejected.
concept.failure_modes: Silent or mis-parsed rejects leave strategies believing they have live orders when they do not - a classic cause of unhedged exposure in automated systems. Rejection cascades during volatility (risk limits tripping) can also block risk-reducing orders.
concept.misconceptions: A rejection is not a partial fill or a failed execution - no quantity traded. And an acknowledgment does not immunize an order from later rejection (e.g., on regulatory or risk grounds).
concept.example: You resend an order reusing a live ClOrdID; the exchange rejects it as a duplicate, and your system must generate a fresh identifier before the order can enter the book.
